query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a cryogenically cooled substrate during the directed energy deposition (DED) of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will lower the build‐plate temperature sufficiently to reduce residual thermal stresses and promote a refined microstructure, thereby improving mechanical properties compared to conventional high-thermal-load regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder with standard feedstock properties for additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Implement a cryogenically cooled substrate (using liquid nitrogen or a similar cryogen) in the DED process to rapidly extract heat from each deposited layer.
generation.conditions: Processing window targeting miniature components with dimensions around 12×12×12 mm under an inert gas environment; deposition parameters similar to standard DED settings except for substrate cooling to near cryogenic temperatures (substantially below ambient), ensuring the melt pool still reaches processing temperatures while the substrate remains cold.
generation.structural_mediator: The rapid heat extraction minimizes thermal gradients and reduces dwell times at high temperatures, leading to a finer, more uniform grain structure with lower dislocation accumulation.
generation.mechanism: By actively cooling the substrate to cryogenic temperatures, the system quickly removes excess heat from the deposited layers. This limits the time available for thermal stress accumulation, reduces grain coarsening, and suppresses the development of residual plastic strain as measured by techniques like Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM).
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with the cryogenically cooled substrate are expected to exhibit statistically significant reductions in residual thermal stresses and improved mechanical strength and toughness relative to those processed under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing, where an insulated but non‐cryogenic substrate leads to prolonged high substrate temperatures that promote residual stress build-up, grain coarsening, and degraded mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention’s effectiveness may be limited to small-scale geometries (around 12×12×12 mm), as overly steep thermal gradients could induce thermal shock or cracking; additional optimization might be required to balance rapid cooling and mechanical integrity.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal cooling rate and thermal gradient necessary to achieve stress relief without inducing deleterious thermal shock. The detailed influence of cryogenic cooling on microstructural evolution in the AlCrFeNiSi system also requires further empirical verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature components (approximately 12×12×12 mm) using the same AlCrFeNiSi DED process: one set with a conventional insulated substrate and another set with an integrated cryogenically cooled substrate. Ensure that all other processing parameters remain identical.
measurements: EBSD analysis for Kernel Average Misorientation to assess residual stress
Mechanical testing (tensile strength, hardness) to compare mechanical properties
SEM analysis to evaluate grain size distribution and microstructural uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components produced with the cryogenically cooled substrate do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stress and improvement in mechanical properties, or if they develop increased incidences of thermal shock-induced cracking compared to the conventional process, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To optimize the deposition conditions, the temperature evolution of the platform (Ti Grade 2, 95 × 95 × 5 mm) was measured using thermocouples welded next to the deposited samples. Placing the titanium platform on a 40-mm-thick ceramic fiber insulating platform Ultraboard 1850-400 (80% Al2O3 + 20% SiO2) (Schupp, Aachen, Germany) with a thermal conductivity of 0.34 W∙m−1∙K−1 was found to effectively suppress heat transfer to the permanently cooled working table of the machine which allows for minimizing cooling rates. Additionally, to achieve greater heat accumulation in the sample, the dwell time between the deposition of adjacent layers was turned off. This deposition strategy proved to reduce negative effects of rapid cooling, such as excessive internal stress, which are known to result in cracking of brittle materials such as RHEAs []. The Insstek MX-Lab apparatus and experimental setup used for deposition on a thermally insulated platform are shown in Figure 2. The temperature evolution during the deposition of bulk samples with and without an insulated plate having nominal dimensions of 12 × 12 × 12 mm is shown in Figure 3a. The present study demonstrates that a strategic combination of deposition-parameters optimization and thermal management enables the fabrication of a crack-free bulk CrNbTiZr RCCA via L-DED using elemental powders. This represents a significant advancement, as prior efforts involving DED of similar systems have typically been limited to thin-wall geometries and have often suffered from severe cracking, substantial residual porosity, or incomplete fusion [,,,,,,]. Our results indicate that insulating the build platform and minimizing the dwell time between the layers elevates the overall temperature of the sample, effectively preventing the formation of macrocracks. It can be attributed to the fact that the deposition on insulated substrate reduces temperature gradients created at the edge of the melt pool which in turn decreases the strain concentrations and suppresses the formation of cracks. In contrast, samples deposited on the thermally conductive platform exhibited pronounced cracking. A laser-induced pre-heating temperature of approximately 500 °C was determined to be adequate to achieve this effect.
